name: Utah
nameStory: From the Ute people, whose name is often given as 'people of the mountains.' The nickname is the stranger one: the beehive stands for industry and cooperative labor, a symbol Mormon settlers chose to describe how they intended to survive in a desert.
capitalStory: In 1847 Brigham Young led Mormon pioneers 1,300 miles west, looked out over a salt flat ringed by mountains, and reportedly said 'This is the right place.' They chose land nobody else wanted precisely because nobody else wanted it - being left alone was the entire point.

funFacts: The Great Salt Lake is a terminal lake: rivers pour in and the only way out is evaporation, so everything dissolved stays behind. That is why it is saltier than the ocean.
It is the shrunken remnant of Lake Bonneville, an ice-age lake that was once the size of Lake Michigan.
Utah has five national parks, more than any state except California.
Utah applied for statehood six times over 46 years and was refused until the LDS church renounced polygamy in 1890.
whyItMatters: The Great Salt Lake has lost most of its volume, and the exposed lakebed contains arsenic and other heavy metals that blow into Salt Lake City as dust. A drying lake is turning into a public health problem for two million people.
